note: Principled agent design patterns with provable injection resistance, the constructive counterpart to the attack literature.
title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
explain_beginner: AI assistants that browse the web, read emails, or run commands on your behalf face a danger called prompt injection. Because these assistants follow instructions written in plain language, an attacker can hide a fake command inside a webpage, document, or email the assistant reads, and the assistant may obey it as if its owner had asked. This could mean an AI email assistant sending your private messages to a stranger, or a coding assistant tricked into running harmful commands. This paper asks whether AI assistants can be built so this trick simply cannot work, rather than just detecting attacks after the fact. The researchers propose six blueprints for structuring an assistant's internal workflow, each closing off the attack a different way, for example by never letting information read from outside sources feed back into decisions about which actions to take. They test the ideas against ten realistic scenarios, from managing a calendar to screening resumes, and find that safety typically comes at the cost of some flexibility.
explain_business: For anyone building or buying an AI agent that reads external content, whether emails, web pages, or customer files, and then takes real actions, prompt injection is a live security risk today, not a theoretical one. This paper offers a menu of architectural choices that reduce or eliminate the risk, but every option costs something. Restricting an agent to a fixed set of actions closes the door to injection but loses flexibility, such as free-form search. Separating a privileged component that can act from a quarantined one that only reads untrusted data limits damage but adds engineering complexity, and the quarantined part can still be fooled internally. The practical takeaway for a business evaluating an AI agent product is to ask the vendor which of these patterns, if any, their system uses, rather than accepting a generic claim of being secure against prompt injection. A vendor relying only on filtering or detection, per the authors, is not offering a real guarantee.
explain_practitioner: The paper frames prompt injection as untrusted content overriding an LLM agent's intended instructions, covering direct injection in user input and indirect injection via tool outputs or documents, with attacker goals from unauthorized tool calls to data exfiltration and code execution. Rather than relying on detectors or adversarial training, which the authors say offer no guarantees, they define six architectural patterns: Action-Selector, restricting the LLM to predefined actions with no feedback from tool outputs. Plan-Then-Execute, fixing the plan before untrusted data is seen. LLM Map-Reduce, isolating per-document processing. Dual LLM, separating a privileged tool-using LLM from a quarantined one with no tool access. Code-Then-Execute, having the LLM emit executable code instead of a plan. And Context-Minimization, stripping prior prompts from context after an action starts. Each is applied across ten case studies, from an OS assistant to a medical diagnosis chatbot. No attack-success numbers are reported, only qualitative analysis. The clearest limitation: no single pattern secures a fully general-purpose agent, and each trades away some dynamic capability for its guarantee.
